summary: This unit teaches you to manage the putting into practice of an approved policy in a Jamaican ministry, agency or municipal corporation. You will learn to study the policy, map and engage stakeholders, build an implementation plan with a Gantt chart, RACI chart, budget and risk register, communicate and train, manage resistance, apply the policy consistently and ethically, monitor progress against indicators, evaluate results and report to senior officers.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to manage **policy implementation**: turning a policy that has been approved into day-to-day practice, so that the people it is meant to help actually feel the difference.

A **policy** is a statement of what government or an organisation has decided to do, and why. Making the policy is one job; **implementing** it is another. Many good policies fail not because the idea was wrong but because nobody planned the tasks, the money, the training or the checking. At Level 5 you are the manager who closes that gap.

**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers in ministries, departments and agencies, statutory bodies and municipal corporations (the parish councils became municipal corporations in 2016), and anyone who may be asked to lead a change that has been decided above them.

What this means in practice
rows: Study its aims, scope, legal basis and who must do what, and ask the policy owner when something is unclear.
Map who is affected or has influence, consult them early and keep them informed.
Set objectives, break the work into tasks, show them on a Gantt chart with milestones, and give each task an owner (RACI).
Prepare and control a budget, ask for what is missing, and keep a risk register with responses.
Tell staff and the public what is changing, train people, and deal with fear and opposition.
Apply the policy consistently and ethically
Write procedures, make sure officers decide alike, declare conflicts and keep proper records.
Set indicators and a baseline, measure progress, take corrective action and report to senior officers.
Judge whether the policy worked, report unintended effects and help improve the policy.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the topics in these notes, including short sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and calculations) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: preparing an implementation plan pack, and holding a review meeting and report on a policy that has been running for six months. You are assessed on your own named role and on your explanation of it.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms and the sums in the Revision section. Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as stakeholder, milestone, outcome, baseline and RACI, and for percentages worked out correctly.

sections.title: Policy, implementation and the legal framework

blocks.p: A policy states **what** is to be achieved and **why**. A **law** is passed by Parliament and must be obeyed. A **programme** is a set of activities that delivers a policy. A **procedure** is the step-by-step way staff carry out a task. A **plan** says who does what, when and with what money. Implementation links them all.

head: Term
What it is
Example
rows: A decision on direction and principles
Every municipal corporation will answer building applications within a set number of working days
The law that set up the municipal corporation and its powers
Activities and projects that deliver the policy
Training, a new tracking system, extra staff at the counter
Receive, log, check against the list, route to the officer, notify the applicant
Tasks, owners, dates, money, risks and measures
A Gantt chart, RACI chart, budget and risk register

blocks.p: The **implementation gap** is the difference between what a policy intends and what actually happens on the ground. It grows when the aims are unclear, staff are not told or trained, the money or equipment does not arrive, nobody is accountable, or the people affected were never asked.
Before you plan anything, read the approved policy and its supporting documents, and write down in your own words:

ul: **Aims**: what change is wanted, and by when.
**Scope**: which offices, services, people and places it covers, and what it does not cover.
**Requirements**: what officers and the public must now do or stop doing.
**Authority**: who approved it, who owns it (the policy unit or the permanent secretary) and who may decide when something is not covered.
**Link to other rules**: employment law, the public service rules, the procurement rules, the data protection law, the access to information law and the agency's own manuals.

blocks.p: If something is unclear, ask the policy owner **before** you start. Do not guess, and do not change the aims to suit your convenience: your job is to deliver the policy, not to rewrite it.

blocks.note: Implementation planning follows understanding. The first action when you are handed a policy is to study its aims, scope and requirements, not to order equipment, announce dates or hold a public meeting.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Identify the problem and agenda
Develop options and decide
Approve the policy
Implement
Monitor progress
Evaluate and review
Feed back to the policy makers

blocks.p: Implementation sits in the middle of this cycle. What you learn while implementing (what works, what does not, who is left out) is valuable and must flow back to the people who own the policy.

You can **delegate tasks**, but you cannot delegate **accountability**. A director who gives work to section heads still answers for the overall result to the permanent secretary or the chief executive. In a ministry the permanent secretary is the accounting officer; in an executive agency or statutory body it is the chief executive officer (CEO), who reports to a board.

blocks.note: Public bodies in Jamaica work under the public financial management law, the procurement rules and the access to information law. Refer to them by what they do. Never quote section numbers or penalties unless your instructor gives them to you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **stakeholder** is any person or group who can **affect**, or is **affected by**, the policy. Missing a stakeholder is one of the commonest causes of failure: a group that was ignored may resist, complain to the media or simply not co-operate.

Think in layers: those inside your body (staff, managers, unions or associations, the board), partners (other agencies, contractors, suppliers), those who use the service (customers, businesses, residents), those who oversee (the ministry, the Minister, auditors, Parliament) and those who comment (the media, civil society, church and community groups).

blocks.h: Step 2: map them on the power-interest grid

head: Power and interest
Low interest
High interest
rows: Keep satisfied: brief them regularly, do not overload them, and make sure they are never surprised
**Manage closely**: involve them in key decisions, meet often, test ideas with them
Monitor: watch for change, send general notices
Keep informed and consult: they care a great deal, so listen, explain, and use their knowledge

blocks.p: **Example.** A municipal corporation is introducing a market-fee policy. The councillors and the finance director (high power, high interest) are managed closely. The vendors' association (high interest, less formal power) is consulted and kept well informed. The tax office, which only needs to be told of any change to the bank account, is kept informed at a low level.

blocks.note: Position on the grid changes over time. A group with low power can gain power by going to the media, the Minister or the courts. Re-check the map at each stage.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Level
What it means
Use it when
rows: One-way: tell them what is happening
The decision is made and people just need to know
Two-way: ask their views before deciding how to implement
You can still change the method (not the aims)
Work with them through the planning
Their know-how will improve the procedure
They have power or resources you need

ul: **Consult early.** Staff and their union or association should hear about a change that affects hours, duties or conditions before it is fixed, in line with employment law and good practice.
Be honest about what **can** be changed (how, when, where) and what **cannot** (the aims of an approved policy).
Keep a **stakeholder register**: who, their interest, their power, what they need, what you will do, who owns the contact, and a record of every meeting.

blocks.note: Consulting does not mean agreeing with everyone. It means listening, using good ideas, and explaining the decision to those who disagree.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **implementation plan** is the single document that tells everybody what will be done, by whom, by when, with what money, and how success will be measured. It should be short enough to read and exact enough to follow.

ul: **Aim and objectives**: written as SMART objectives (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound).
**Baseline**: where things stand now.
**Tasks and milestones** with start and end dates.
**Owners**: who is responsible and who is accountable for each task.
**Resources**: staff, money, equipment, space, systems.
**Risks** and how they will be managed.
**Communication and training plan.**
**Monitoring and reporting arrangements**: indicators, targets and how often.
**Governance**: a project team or steering group, with its meeting dates.

blocks.h: Work breakdown: from the aim to tasks

flow: State the objective
Split it into main work areas (systems, forms, training, communication)
Break each into tasks small enough for one owner
Estimate the time and cost of each task
Find which tasks depend on others
Put them in order on a Gantt chart

blocks.p: A **Gantt chart** is a bar chart: tasks run down the side, time runs across the top, and a bar shows when each task starts and finishes. It shows the **order** and **timing** of the work, the **dependencies** (task B cannot start until task A is done) and the **milestones**. A **milestone** is a checkpoint that marks the end of a key stage, for example 'procedures approved' or 'staff training complete'.

blocks.h: Worked example: finding the shortest time

blocks.p: A municipal corporation will launch a new application-tracking procedure. The tasks are:

head: Task
Weeks
Starts after
rows: E. Review the pilot and fix problems
Can run at any time, must end by launch

blocks.p: The longest chain of dependent tasks is A (4) + B or C (3) + D (4) + E (2) = **13 weeks**. This is the **critical path**: a delay to any task on it delays the launch. B and C run side by side, so the 3 weeks for each count only once. Task F is not on the critical path: it has **float** (spare time), so it can start any time within the 13 weeks as long as it finishes by the launch. If training (C) slips by 2 weeks, it becomes 5 weeks and the whole project takes 15 weeks, because C is now the longer of the two parallel tasks.

blocks.note: Always add the durations along each chain and compare the chains. The longest chain sets the earliest finish date. Check the sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Working backwards from a fixed date.** A policy starts in 20 weeks. Training takes 3 weeks and must finish 2 weeks before the start. Training must therefore end at week 18 and start at week 15, which is 15 weeks from now.

When a policy needs a system change, new forms and staff training, the sensible order is: design the system and forms, test them, then train staff on what they will really use, then launch. Training people on a system that is still changing wastes time and confuses them.

head: Approach
What it means
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Try the new procedure in one office or area first
Testing procedures, finding problems cheaply, building confidence
A pilot site that is not typical gives misleading results
Introduce it office by office or stage by stage
Large or risky changes, limited training staff
Offices in different phases give different service for a time
Small bodies, or where two systems cannot run together
Any fault hits everybody; needs a tested back-up

blocks.p: **Example of phasing.** A policy rolled out to 14 parishes at 2 parishes a month, beginning in January, reaches the last parish in the **7th month, July** (14 ÷ 2 = 7 months; January is month 1).

A **RACI chart** shows, for each task, who is **R**esponsible (does the work), **A**ccountable (answers for it and has the final say; only **one** person per task), **C**onsulted (asked before; two-way) and **I**nformed (told afterwards; one-way).

blocks.note: If a task has two accountable people, nobody is accountable. If it has none, nobody will be. If it has many 'R's and no one to chase them, it will drift.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Set up a small **implementation team** (or steering group) that meets regularly, decides on problems, approves changes and reports upward. When several bodies must act together, for example the police, the transport authority and the municipal corporations on a road-safety policy, use a **joint group with agreed roles and shared targets**, not separate efforts.

blocks.note: A plan is a tool, not a ritual. If the policy reaches its date but the plan was followed word for word and the aim was missed, the plan has failed.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Check what the plan needs against what you have: **people** (numbers and skills), **money**, **equipment and systems**, **space**, **time**. If there is a gap, do not hide it and do not simply fail. Set out the gap clearly, with **costed options**, and take it to your director or the policy owner for decision. Options might be: more staff, a longer timeline, a narrower first phase, or a smaller scope agreed in writing.

A budget is needed because public money must be approved and controlled before it is spent. Typical lines are staff time and overtime, training, equipment and software, printing and communication, travel, monitoring and evaluation, and a **contingency** (a reserve for the unexpected, often 5 to 10 per cent, depending on the risk and the body's rules).
**Worked example.** An agency has a budget of J$6,000,000. It plans training J$2,000,000, systems J$2,200,000 and communication J$500,000.

If the systems supplier then raises its price by 20%, the increase is 20% of J$2,200,000 = **J$440,000**. Contingency falls to J$860,000. Ask whether the rise is allowed by the contract and the procurement rules, look for savings, and tell your director.

head: Measure
How to work it
Example
rows: Budget for the period - actual spend

blocks.p: Compare **spending** with **progress**. If 65% of the budget is spent but only 50% of the work is done, the project is heading for an overspend even though the budget line looks healthy.

A **risk** is something that may happen and, if it does, would harm the implementation. A **risk register** lists each risk with its **likelihood**, its **impact**, a **rating**, the **response**, the **owner** and the **date reviewed**.

head: Risk
Likelihood (1-5)
Impact (1-5)
Rating
Response
Owner
rows: Staff not trained by the start date
Book training now; record attendance; plan a make-up session
Test early with real users; keep a paper back-up
Fix the price in the contract; hold contingency
Public does not know about the change

blocks.p: **Rating = likelihood × impact.** Colour the ratings: high (for example 15 to 25) red, medium (6 to 14) amber, low (1 to 5) green. The cut-offs vary, so use your agency's own.

head: Response
Meaning
Example
rows: Change the plan so the risk cannot happen
Do not launch in the hurricane season peak
Lower the likelihood or the impact
Test the system; train extra staff
Pass the cost to someone else
Insurance; a contract that makes the supplier pay for its delays
Do nothing now but watch it
A small cost increase within contingency

blocks.note: A good risk entry is specific ('Staff may not be trained by the start date'), not vague ('things may go wrong'). Review the register at every team meeting.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **communication plan** sets out the key messages, audiences, channels, timing and who is responsible. Good messages say **what is changing, why, when, and what it means for the person reading**, including where to go for help.

head: Audience
What they need
Channels
When
rows: Briefings, a question-and-answer sheet, team meetings, notice boards, staff email
First: staff should hear before the public
What changes for them, when, how to get help
Notices at offices, the website and social media, local radio, leaflets, community meetings
Early notice, repeated near the date
Regularly, and straight away for serious problems

ul: Use **several channels**. Many people, especially in rural areas, do not use the internet.
Keep the message **simple and consistent**. Everyone should hear the same facts.
Plan **two-way** channels: a telephone line, a suggestion box, questions at meetings. You learn what is going wrong from the replies.

blocks.p: Training is more effective when it is **short, practical and based on real cases** than when it is a long lecture. Train close to the start date (so it is not forgotten) but early enough for staff to practise and for you to fix gaps. Check understanding by having staff **work through a case and reviewing it**, not just by asking whether they have understood. Keep attendance records and arrange make-up sessions for those who were absent.

head: Cause
What it sounds like
What helps
rows: Fear of loss (job, status, skills, security)
Honest information; clear statements about jobs; training and support
'I heard they are closing us down.'
Frequent, direct communication; a rumour-correcting Q&A
Check whether it is true; adjust workloads; remove old tasks
Listen; explain the reasons; use good ideas; report valid concerns upward
'We have always done it this way.'
Involve people in the design; show quick wins

flow: Listen to the concerns
Check whether they are valid
Respond with facts, support or a change to how (not whether) it is done
Involve staff in planning the details
Recognise early successes

blocks.note: The first move when staff resist is to **listen and find out whether the concern is real**. Ordering, threatening or ignoring them hardens resistance. If the concern is valid (for example a genuine workload problem), fix it or report it. If it is based on rumour, correct it with facts.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **change champion** is a respected colleague who understands the policy, explains it in everyday language, answers questions, collects concerns and shows how it works in practice. Choose people whom staff already trust, not only senior people. Give them proper training and time.

**Involving staff in planning how it will work** is the single most powerful way to gain acceptance, because people support what they help to shape. Be clear about the limits: they can shape the method, not the aims of an approved policy.

sections.title: Applying the policy consistently, fairly and openly

blocks.p: A policy tells staff what to achieve; **procedures** tell them how, day by day. Good procedures give the steps in order, decision rules (for example 'waive the fee if ... '), the forms to use, who may approve, time limits and worked examples.
Two officers in two offices must reach the **same decision on the same facts**. When they do not, customers are treated unfairly and trust falls.

flow: Write clear criteria and a checklist
Train everyone with the same material
Give a named contact for questions and log the answers
Share the log with all offices
Check samples of decisions
Retrain where officers differ

blocks.p: **If officers apply a rule differently**, the manager should clarify the criteria and retrain both officers, not ask each to carry on in their own way.

blocks.h: When a case is not covered

blocks.p: An officer should **not** invent a rule. The case is referred to the person with authority to decide (a supervisor, the policy unit) and the **decision and reasons are recorded** so that the same decision is made next time. If the same type of case keeps arising, tell the policy owner: the procedure may need to be amended.

blocks.h: If applying the rules word for word would defeat the policy

blocks.p: Sometimes a procedure, applied exactly, would stop the policy from reaching its stated aim in some cases. Do **not** quietly ignore the rule and do not follow it blindly. **Raise the issue with the person who can authorise a change, propose a fix, and wait for a written amendment.**

ul: **Declare** any personal or financial interest in a decision (for example a relative or a business that benefits) and **step back** from that decision. Record that you did so.
**Refuse** requests from a politician, friend or colleague to move one person ahead of others or to bend the criteria. Explain that the process applies to everyone, and tell your superior.
Treat all customers by the same rules. Do not accept gifts or favours from people who deal with your office.

blocks.note: Senior public servants must be politically neutral. They serve any government fairly. This is what lets the public trust the service.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep the **decisions, reasons and changes** made during implementation. They show accountability and are needed for later reviews and audits.
Keep minutes and a decision log, and file them where they can be found.

A request for documents from a journalist or citizen is handled **under the access to information law**, with any lawful exemptions, and not refused or ignored by the officer who receives it. Pass it to the officer responsible and follow the agency's procedure.
Protect personal data. Share it only as the data protection law and your agency's rules allow.

blocks.p: **Monitoring** is the regular checking of progress while implementation is going on: are tasks on time and within budget, and are results moving towards the targets? Its purpose is to spot problems early and act.

head: Level
Question
Example (new policy: faster certificates)
rows: What did we produce or deliver?
Certificates issued within a set number of working days
What difference did it make for people?
Families receive documents on time; fewer complaints; higher satisfaction

blocks.p: An **output** counts what the service delivered. An **outcome** measures the **change for people**. A policy is judged on outcomes, but outputs are easier to count while you are implementing.

A **baseline** is the starting measurement, taken **before** the change, so that later results can be compared. Without it you cannot show progress. A **target** is the level you want to reach by a set date. A **milestone** is a stage checkpoint.

blocks.h: The sums: percentage, percentage of target and percentage points

head: Sum
How
Worked example
rows: 960 inspections done against a target of 1,200: 80%
From 60% to 78% on time: 18 percentage points
Contract of J$4,000,000 rises by J$500,000: 12.5%

blocks.note: A change from 60% to 78% is **18 percentage points**, not '18 per cent'. The second would be a percentage change of 30% (18 ÷ 60). Use the right term and say which you mean.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: RAG ratings and the progress report

blocks.p: A **RAG rating** colours progress: **Green** (on track), **Amber** (some slippage, being managed), **Red** (off track, needs a decision or help). Example thresholds are green at 90% or more of plan, amber at 70% to 89%, red below 70%; use your agency's own rules.

A progress report to the permanent secretary should be short and cover: **progress against milestones and targets**, **budget**, **issues**, **risks**, **actions and decisions needed**, and anything unexpected. Use a table for figures and plain sentences for the story.

For a large implementation lasting two years, the best arrangement is **regular progress reports measured against milestones** (for example monthly team reports and quarterly reports upward), not a single check at the end.
**Slippage** is the amount by which work falls behind the plan. When milestones are late:

flow: Find out the causes (not who to blame)
Decide the effect on the end date and cost
Plan recovery: more resources, a changed order, a reduced scope
Agree the plan with those who must act
Report it upward with the recovery plan
Check that the recovery is working

blocks.p: Policies can have effects nobody planned. For example, a rule that all payments must be made online may leave elderly or rural customers unable to pay. When monitoring reveals this, **report it to the policy makers and propose a fix**, and where people are being harmed, put a short-term protection in place (for example an assisted payment point) while the longer-term answer is agreed.

blocks.note: Collect feedback from users and staff as well as figures. Numbers show how much; people tell you why.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Evaluation, review and sustaining the change

head: Feature
Monitoring
Evaluation
rows: Did the policy achieve its aims, and was it worth it?
At set points: mid-term, end, or one year on
The team, an independent officer or an outside evaluator
Lessons, changes to the policy, decisions to continue or stop

head: Criterion
Question
Example measure
rows: Is it still the right response to the problem?
Target met; outcome change from the baseline
Were the results worth the resources?
Did it reach everyone it should, including the vulnerable?
Results by area, age and sex
Is it in budgets, procedures and training?

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A youth-training policy spent J$18,000,000 and 360 young people completed the course. Cost per completer: 18,000,000 ÷ 360 = **J$50,000**. Six months later 240 were in work: 240 ÷ 360 = **66.7%**. If young women are half of the unemployed in those districts but only 12% of trainees, the policy has an **equity** problem, even if the overall figures look good.

The most balanced evaluation uses **results data plus feedback from users and staff**. Where an evaluation finds that a policy works in the towns but not in rural districts, the sensible recommendation is to **adapt delivery to the rural barriers** (distance, transport, internet, language), not to drop the policy or ignore the gap.

The agency that implements must tell the ministry's policy unit what is and is not working: problems with the wording, unworkable requirements, unintended effects, and what it would cost to fix them. This is how a policy improves. Do it through a report, with evidence and a proposal.

When the project team is disbanded, the policy must carry on. Build it into **procedures, job descriptions, induction of new staff, appraisal and budgets**. Leaving a policy dependent on one enthusiastic person means it fades when that person moves.

ul: Hand over to a named permanent owner.
Update manuals and forms.
Keep a light monitoring system going.
Hold a lessons-learned meeting and file the report.
Thank and recognise the people who made it work.

c1.title: Waste-separation policy in May Pen
c1.text: The Municipal Corporation of Clarendon has approved a policy that restaurants, shops and market vendors in the May Pen town centre must separate plastic bottles from other waste, starting in 24 weeks. Andre Thompson, a senior officer, is asked to lead implementation. The people affected include about 150 businesses, the market vendors' association, the waste-collection contractor, public health inspectors and the corporation's finance officer. The contractor decides whether the trucks can collect separately.

c2.title: Electronic leave system at a ministry
c2.text: A ministry's corporate services division is introducing a policy that all staff leave must be applied for and approved through a new electronic system. The implementation budget is J$9,500,000 over 16 weeks, including a contingency of 5% of the budget. After 10 weeks, J$6,175,000 has been spent and the project manager, Kerry-Ann Brown, estimates that half of the planned work is complete.

c3.title: Reply-to-letters policy at an agency
c3.text: An agency's new service policy says every letter from the public must be answered within 10 working days. Before the policy, a sample of 400 letters showed that 208 were answered within 10 working days. After six months, a sample of 450 letters showed that 342 were answered on time. The target for the end of the first year is 90%. Staff in the Montego Bay office are still at 60%.

c4.title: New checklist policy at a land titles office
c4.text: Mrs Pauline Walters manages a land titles office where a new policy requires every application to be checked against a standard checklist and scanned. Long-serving counter staff are saying that scanning is the first step towards cutting jobs, and a rumour is spreading that two offices will close. Several staff say they have never used a scanner. Go-live is in six weeks.

c5.title: Decisions on building applications
c5.text: A municipal corporation's building approvals section has a policy to decide each application within 30 working days using a published list of requirements. Mrs Sonia Reid, the manager, finds that one officer asks every applicant for a surveyor's report, while another asks only some. A councillor telephones her and asks her to 'look after' an application from a local supporter, ahead of those waiting longer.

c6.title: Rural youth-training policy review
c6.text: A youth-training policy was put into practice in six rural districts for two years. It cost J$18,000,000, and 360 young people completed the course. Six months after the course, 240 of them were in work. Young women were half of the unemployed youth in those districts but only 12% of those who enrolled. Officers report that distance to the training centre and lack of transport kept many away.

questions.q: Andre has the approved policy in his hand. Before drawing up dates or buying anything, what should he do first?
o: Read the policy closely and clarify with its owner anything unclear
Choose the pilot area, announce the start date to businesses and then work out the tasks
Meet the contractor and ask how soon the trucks can begin collecting plastic separately
Write the budget request for new bins, because money is always the first thing to be settled
questions.why: Implementation depends on knowing exactly what the policy requires, for whom and by when. Dates, money and contacts follow once he understands that.

questions.q: Using the power-interest grid, how should Andre treat the waste-collection contractor, whose agreement decides whether the policy can work?
o: Keep it informed with a general notice, since it has no say in the policy
Monitor it occasionally, because contractors are paid to do as they are told
Keep it satisfied but avoid sharing early details of the plan with it
Manage closely and involve it in planning decisions
questions.why: The contractor has high power and high interest, so it belongs in the 'manage closely' box and should help to plan the collection method.

questions.q: Andre wants to test the new separation procedures in one section of the town before the whole town is covered. What is the main reason for a pilot?
o: To prove to businesses that the corporation will punish those who refuse
To shorten the plan, because the rest of the town will then need no preparation
To test the procedures and fix problems cheaply before roll-out
To save on the budget, since the pilot area will not need bins or notices
questions.why: A pilot shows what works and what does not on a small scale, so that mistakes are found early and put right before they affect everyone.

questions.q: What percentage of the J$9,500,000 budget has been spent after 10 weeks, and what does it suggest when set beside the progress?
o: 65%, and it suggests the project is ahead of schedule, because spending is high
65%, and it suggests an overspend if work continues at the same cost rate
62.5%, and it suggests the project is exactly on track against the plan
45%, and it suggests the project is under budget with room to spare
questions.why: 6,175,000 ÷ 9,500,000 × 100 = 65%. With only about half the work done, the project has used more than half its money. At this rate it will run over budget.

questions.q: How large is the contingency in the budget, and how much of it would be left after a J$300,000 price rise in the system supplier's bill?
o: J$300,000 and nothing
questions.why: 5% of 9,500,000 = 475,000. Taking away 300,000 leaves 175,000. The manager should then ask the supplier to justify the rise and tell her director that the reserve is much thinner.

questions.q: A risk register entry says: 'Supplier may not deliver the system on time; likelihood 4, impact 5.' What is the rating, and what does it tell Kerry-Ann?
o: 20, a high rating that needs a response and an owner now
9, a medium rating that she can leave until the next review
20, which only means the risk is certain to happen
9, which means the impact is smaller than the likelihood
questions.why: Rating = likelihood × impact = 4 × 5 = 20, near the top of the scale. High-rated risks need a named owner and a response such as a fixed delivery date in the contract, or a back-up plan.

questions.q: What was the baseline, and by how many percentage points has performance improved after six months?
o: 76% and 24 points
60% and 16 points
52% and 24 points
questions.why: 208 ÷ 400 = 52%; 342 ÷ 450 = 76%. 76 - 52 = 24 percentage points. Say 'points' because the change is a difference between two percentages.

questions.q: What percentage of the 90% target has the agency reached after six months, to the nearest whole per cent?
questions.why: 76 ÷ 90 × 100 = 84.4%, so 84%. The gap that remains is 90 - 76 = 14 percentage points. Do not mix up 'percentage of target' with the percentage achieved.

questions.q: Which of these is an OUTCOME indicator for the reply-to-letters policy?
o: The number of letters answered by each officer in a month
The number of staff trained to use the new letter-tracking form
The change in how many citizens say they got a clear, timely reply
The amount of money spent on printing and postage for replies
questions.why: An outcome is the difference the policy makes to people. The other options count inputs, activities or outputs.

questions.q: The Montego Bay office is still at 60% on-time replies against a plan of 90%. What should the implementation manager do first?
o: Replace the Montego Bay office manager before looking at the cause
Find the causes there, agree a recovery plan with the office and report it upward
Wait for the next annual evaluation, since the monitoring figures are only a guide
Remove the office's figures from the report so that the overall result looks better
questions.why: Corrective action begins with finding the cause, such as staffing, backlog or system problems, then a recovery plan with owners and dates, and honest reporting.

questions.q: Mrs Walters hears staff say scanning will cost jobs and that two offices will close. What is the best first response?
o: Listen, check what is true and give staff the facts, including what is and is not decided
Tell staff the rumours are foolish and that the policy will go ahead whatever they think
Delay the policy for six months until staff stop worrying about it
Send a written warning to those who repeat the rumour, to stop it spreading
questions.why: Resistance based on fear and rumour is best met by listening and by clear, honest, repeated information. Ordering or punishing hardens resistance.

questions.q: Which action will best prepare the counter staff who have never used a scanner?
o: A one-hour talk on the policy's history, held on the first day of go-live
A printed instruction sheet posted on the notice board with no practice
Training for supervisors only, who will then show the others as they go
Practical sessions on the real equipment, with real cases, before go-live
questions.why: Practice on the real equipment with real cases is the most effective, and it must finish early enough for gaps to be fixed before go-live.

questions.q: How can a change champion best help in this office?
o: As a senior officer who gives the orders and records who has not complied
As an outside consultant who writes the checklist and leaves before go-live
As the staff member who is most opposed, so that others will see the problem
As a trusted colleague who explains it simply and passes on concerns
questions.why: A champion is respected by colleagues, understands the policy, explains it simply and brings back what staff are worried about. Trust matters more than rank.

questions.q: Two officers ask for different documents from applicants. What should Mrs Reid do?
o: Let each officer carry on, since applicants all get an answer in the end
Choose the officer who asks for more documents and tell the other to copy
Clarify the criteria in a written checklist and retrain both officers
Wait for complaints from applicants before she changes anything
questions.why: Consistent application means the same decision on the same facts. A written checklist and training for everyone remove the difference.

questions.q: The councillor asks Mrs Reid to 'look after' a supporter's application. What is the best response?
o: Agree to look at it quietly, as long as the application meets the requirements
Decline openly, say the same process applies to all, and tell her director
Refuse, but give the councillor a list of the other applicants to show it is fair
Pass the application to a junior officer so that she cannot be blamed
questions.why: Political pressure must be declined openly; decisions follow the published process for everyone. Recording and reporting the request protects the officer and the office.

questions.q: Why should the section keep a record of each decision and the reasons for it?
o: To show accountability and allow review, audit and consistent decisions
To give the councillor evidence that his supporters were treated unfairly
To reduce the number of officers needed to make the decisions
To make sure that no applicant ever asks for a decision to be reviewed
questions.why: Records show who decided what and why. They support audits, appeals and the access to information law, and help officers decide similar cases in the same way.

questions.q: What was the cost per completer, and what does it measure?
o: J$50,000, a measure of efficiency
J$50,000, a measure of equity
J$75,000, a measure of effectiveness
J$30,000, a measure of relevance
questions.why: 18,000,000 ÷ 360 = 50,000. Cost per person reached measures efficiency: whether the results justified the resources used.

questions.q: The review team wants to say the policy was fair to everyone it should reach. Which finding most challenges that claim?
o: Two-thirds of those who completed the course were later in work
The course cost J$50,000 for each person who completed it
The policy was introduced in six districts instead of one
Young women were half the unemployed but only 12% of those enrolled
questions.why: Equity asks whether the policy reached everyone it should, including groups in need. The very low share of young women is an equity gap, whatever the overall employment result.

questions.q: A policy goes live in 18 weeks. The pilot takes 4 weeks and the review of the pilot takes 2 weeks. The review must finish 3 weeks before go-live. In how many weeks from now must the pilot start?
o: Week 12
Week 11
Week 9
Week 6
questions.why: Work back from week 18: the review ends at week 15, so it starts at week 13; the 4-week pilot must then start at week 9. Forgetting the 3-week gap gives week 12; forgetting the review gives week 11.

questions.q: In a RACI chart for a policy roll-out, two senior officers are each marked 'A' for the same task. What is the problem?
o: The task will be done twice, because both officers must do the work
Accountability is unclear, because only one person should answer for each task
Neither officer needs to be told about progress on the task
The chart is correct, since two accountable officers give extra safety
questions.why: Accountable means the one person who answers for the task and has the final say. With two, each can assume the other will act, and no one is really accountable.
